title: AI legal research: how reliable is it and how to test it
description: How AI legal research tools find cases and answer legal questions, what Stanford researchers found about errors, and how to check a tool before relying on it.
summary: AI legal research tools answer legal questions in plain language and point to cases and statutes. They save time on first-pass research, but they can state the law wrongly or cite a source that does not support the claim.

example.input: Does a non-compete agreement signed in Texas hold up when the employee moves to California?
example.output: A short answer with the cases and statutes relied on, each with a link, and a note on where the law is unsettled.

howToTest: Write 30 questions your lawyers already answered, including some with a false premise built into the question.
Run each question and have a lawyer check every cited case: does it exist, and does it say what the tool claims?
Count two kinds of errors separately: a wrong statement of law, and a correct statement that cites a source that does not support it.
Include questions about recent changes in the law and about a specific state, where tools tend to be weaker.
Record how often it says it does not know, which is the right answer to some questions.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a legal research product built on a real case database. It has the sources and the citations to check.
buyVsBuild.build: Build only when you have a private body of documents, such as your own past memos, and an engineer to maintain it.

watchOuts: Stanford researchers tested two leading legal research tools in 2024 and found incorrect information more than 17% of the time for Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI, and more than 34% for Westlaw AI-Assisted Research.
In the same work, earlier tests of general-purpose chatbots found hallucination rates between 58% and 82% on legal queries.
A New York lawyer faced sanctions for citing cases a chatbot invented. A lawyer must check every citation.
Those results are from 2024 tests. Tools change, so test the current version yourself.

resources.name: Stanford HAI: AI on Trial, Legal Models Hallucinate
resources.what: A summary of Stanford RegLab and HAI research that tested legal AI research tools on over 200 open-ended legal queries.

sources.name: Stanford HAI: AI on Trial (May 23, 2024)
sources.what: Reports that tested legal research tools produced incorrect information in more than 17% to more than 34% of queries, and describes wrong answers and misgrounded citations as two types of hallucination.
